tools.name: File Type Detector
tools.description: Detect real file types from magic bytes and flag extension/MIME mismatches, macros and polyglot files across folders.
tools.engine: Go + gabriel-vasile/mimetype + own ZIP/OLE2 container, polyglot and file-name checks
tools.engine_reason: Pure-Go magic-byte detection for ~200 formats in one static binary: no libmagic, no ONNX runtime (Magika was evaluated and rejected for that reason).
tools.release_notes: Detects ISO 9660/UDF, DMG, VHD/VHDX, VMDK and QCOW images; archive entries that run on double-click are warn, risk only when disguised or inside an archive posing as another type; text starting with MZ is text; Unicode whitespace padding caught in double extensions; .winmd accepted; EPUB without a mimetype entry detected.

howto: Open File Type Detector (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47101).
Drop one or more files on the page, or press "Choose a folder" to scan a whole folder.
Press Scan. Risky files are listed first, with the reason for each flag.
Download the results as JSON or CSV.
From a terminal or CI job: localtools-file-type-detector scan <folder> --fail-on risk exits with code 2 when a risky file is found.

faqs.q: How does it know the real type if the extension is wrong?
faqs.a: It reads the first bytes of each file (the magic number) and matches them against about 200 known signatures using the mimetype library, then looks inside ZIP and OLE containers. The file name is only used to check for mismatches.

faqs.q: What counts as a risky file?
faqs.a: An executable or script named like a document or image, an Office file with VBA macros, an archive that contains executables, a polyglot (for example a PDF that is also a valid ZIP), a double extension like photo.jpg.exe, or a name with a right-to-left override character.

faqs.q: Can I use it in CI to block uploads?
faqs.a: Yes. Run localtools-file-type-detector scan <path> --fail-on risk (or --fail-on warn). It exits with code 2 when a file reaches that level, and --json or --csv gives machine-readable output.

faqs.q: Are my files uploaded anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The page talks only to the local server on 127.0.0.1, and the tool makes no network requests. Uploaded files are deleted when the request finishes.

faqs.q: Why not Google Magika?
faqs.a: Magika needs the ONNX Runtime library, which would turn a single small static binary into a large native bundle, and it is strongest at text and source-code types. The risky formats here (executables, Office containers, archives) have exact byte signatures, so signature matching is faster and explains its answer.

tools.name: PDF Toolkit
tools.description: Merge, split, reorder, rotate, compress, stamp, number, encrypt and fill PDF forms, offline.
tools.engine: Go + pdfcpu, plus own image recompression, form flattening and XFDF/FDF import
tools.engine_reason: pdfcpu is a pure-Go PDF library covering merge, split, pages, rotate, optimize, stamps, AES-256 and AcroForm fill in one static binary; no Ghostscript, qpdf or Java.
tools.release_notes: Fixes clipped Latin form appearances in short LibreOffice widgets; rich-text plain-value fallback and per-cell comb appearances; exact numeric JSON values; ordinary indirect uncompressed FDF; immediate stale UI result/field clearing, async response cancellation/guards, and encrypted-form password retry. Adds independent rendered-ink and comb-geometry regressions. Existing worker isolation and documented non-WinAnsi flattening limits remain.

howto: Open PDF Toolkit (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47102).
Pick the operation: Merge, Split, Pages, Rotate, Compress, Stamp, Numbers, Encrypt, Decrypt, Metadata or Forms.
Drop your PDF (several for Merge, then order them and set page ranges per file).
Set the options shown for that operation and press the button.
Check the page count and size, then download the result. From a terminal: localtools-pdf-toolkit merge a.pdf b.pdf -o out.pdf.

faqs.q: Does compress really make files smaller?
faqs.a: Lossless mode removes duplicate and unused objects, which helps on bloated files but not on tight ones (the original is returned if nothing smaller is found). Medium and strong also downsample large photos and re-encode them as JPEG, which is where most of the size goes: a photo PDF went from 1.7 MB to 246 KB in testing. Line art, screenshots, CMYK and 1-bit images are left untouched.

faqs.q: How do I fill a PDF form automatically?
faqs.a: Run localtools-pdf-toolkit export form.pdf > data.json to get every field with its current value, edit the values, then localtools-pdf-toolkit fill form.pdf data.json -o filled.pdf. XFDF and FDF files exported from Acrobat work too, and --flatten bakes the values into the page.

faqs.q: Which encryption does it use?
faqs.a: AES-256. Where the file can be written as PDF 2.0 it uses the PDF 2.0 standard handler (revision 6); otherwise the older AES-256 scheme (revision 5), and the result tells you which. You can set a password to open the file, an owner password, and whether printing, copying, commenting and editing are allowed.

faqs.q: Can it handle large files?
faqs.a: Yes, up to about 400 MB in the app. A 1200-page PDF rotates in under a second and a 200 MB file in about 1.5 s. The whole document is held in memory (about 5x the file size at peak), each job may use up to 2 GiB, and at most two jobs run at once.

faqs.q: Are my PDFs uploaded?
faqs.a: No. The page only talks to the local server on 127.0.0.1, the tool makes no network requests, and uploaded files are deleted as soon as each request finishes.

tools.name: PDF Diff
tools.description: Compare two PDFs page by page with visual pixel-diff overlays and a text diff.
tools.engine: Python + PDFium (pypdfium2 5.14) render/text/structure + Pillow pixel diff + difflib word diff
tools.engine_reason: PDFium renders pages exactly like Chrome and gives text with character boxes; Pillow compares pixels in C and difflib diffs words, so no numpy is needed.
tools.release_notes: PDFium 8076 (pypdfium2 5.14.0) replaces PDFium 6462, which had later memory-safety CVEs. Scanned PDFs with inserted or removed pages now pair quickly: each thumbnail is rendered once and unchanged pages anchor the pairing. Visual diff is faster. The render budget is now the measured 100 megapixels per PDF. Damaged pages and unusable page sizes get clear errors, out-of-memory is reported as the memory budget, and the word-change list shows operators without ligatures.

howto: Choose PDF A (the original) and PDF B (the revised version). Enter a password only if a PDF is encrypted.
Pick a mode: Visual compares rendered pixels, Text compares words in reading order, Structure compares metadata, fonts, annotations, form fields, bookmarks and attachments.
For Visual, set the resolution and how much colour difference to ignore; keep Ignore anti-aliasing on to skip edge noise and 1-pixel shifts.
Press Compare, then open any page pair from the list. Switch between Side by side, Diff and Slider, and jump with Prev/Next change.
Download the highlighted report PDF, a ZIP of PNGs of the changed pages, or the JSON summary.

faqs.q: What if pages were inserted or removed?
faqs.a: When the page counts differ, pages are paired by content (word overlap, or thumbnails for scanned pages), so the extra pages show up as inserted or deleted and the rest still line up.

faqs.q: Does it work on scanned PDFs?
faqs.a: Visual mode does: it compares the page images. Text mode needs a text layer, and there is no OCR.

faqs.q: Can I use it in scripts or CI?
faqs.a: Yes. localtools-pdf-diff a.pdf b.pdf --mode text --json prints a JSON summary; the exit code is 0 when the PDFs match, 1 when they differ and 2 on error. --report and --png-zip write the exports.

faqs.q: What are the limits?
faqs.a: 64 MiB and 2,000 pages per PDF, 100 megapixels rendered per PDF per comparison (about 105 Letter pages at 100 DPI), 120 seconds per comparison and two comparisons at a time. Each comparison runs in a worker process that is killed when it runs too long.

faqs.q: Are my files uploaded anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The tool runs on your computer and only talks to your own browser on 127.0.0.1; nothing is sent over the network.

tools.name: PDF to Markdown
tools.description: Convert PDFs to clean Markdown and JSONL chunks for RAG, keeping tables and reading order.
tools.engine_reason: docling (MIT) recovers layout, tables and reading order far better than plain text extraction.

tools.name: CSV SQL Query
tools.description: Run SQL on CSV, TSV, JSON, Parquet and log files (nginx, Apache, syslog) with DuckDB.
tools.engine: DuckDB 1.5.6 (official CLI, bundled) + log parsers (nginx/Apache, syslog RFC 3164/5424)
tools.engine_reason: DuckDB queries CSV/Parquet/JSON in place, in parallel and out of core: a 1 GB CSV aggregates in about 1-2 s. The official CLI is bundled with the excel and sqlite extensions, so it works offline on every OS without cgo.
tools.release_notes: Fix: after a one-page result, paging a larger result could stop at rows 201-400.

fields.sql: SELECT c.name, count(*) AS n FROM orders o JOIN customers c USING (customer_id) GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY n DESC, c.name LIMIT 1

howto: Run localtools-csv-sql-query (or open CSV SQL Query from your app menu); it opens in your browser.
Drop one or more files: CSV, TSV, JSON/JSONL, Parquet, XLSX, SQLite, or nginx/Apache/syslog logs. Each becomes a table named after the file, with its columns and types listed.
Write SQL (DuckDB dialect) or click one of the example queries built from your columns, then press Run or Ctrl+Enter.
Page through the result, check the plan with Explain or Explain analyze, and download the result as CSV, JSON, Parquet or XLSX.
From a terminal: localtools-csv-sql-query query "SELECT ..." data.csv logs/access.log -o out.parquet, or localtools-csv-sql-query shell data.csv for an interactive DuckDB shell.

faqs.q: How big can the files be?
faqs.a: Multi-gigabyte files work: DuckDB streams them and spills to disk. On a Windows laptop a 1 GB, 12-million-row CSV counts in 1.9 s and a GROUP BY with COUNT DISTINCT takes 1.2 s using under 1 GB of memory. In the browser, results of any size are paged 200 rows at a time.

faqs.q: Which log formats are understood?
faqs.a: nginx and Apache access logs (combined and common), syslog in RFC 3164 (with or without <PRI>, classic or RFC 3339 timestamps) and RFC 5424, and JSON-lines logs. They become typed tables (status INTEGER, time TIMESTAMPTZ, ...) with a line_no column; lines that do not match are counted and reported. Any other text file becomes a table of lines.

faqs.q: Can I join files of different formats?
faqs.a: Yes. Every file is a table in the same DuckDB database, so you can join a CSV with a Parquet file, a sheet of an .xlsx and an access log in one query. SQLite and DuckDB files are attached read-only as name.table.

faqs.q: Does my data leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs locally with no network access: extension autoloading is off, and in the web UI DuckDB is locked to the uploaded files (it cannot read other paths, fetch URLs or change that setting). Session files are deleted when you close the page.

faqs.q: Why does my query fail with a line and column?
faqs.a: Errors come straight from DuckDB and are mapped to the position in your SQL; the UI selects the offending spot in the editor. For CSV data errors DuckDB reports the line number in the file.

tools.name: CSV JSON Transform
tools.description: Convert and transform CSV, TSV, JSON and JSONL with Miller verbs: filter, sort, join, reshape.
tools.engine_reason: Miller 6 is pure Go, embeddable, and its verbs (filter, sort, join, reshape) are already well known.
tools.release_notes: Security fix: verb chain validated with Miller's own parser; all DSL redirects, main flags in put/filter and --prepipe refused in the web UI/API.

howto: Drop a CSV, TSV, JSON or JSON Lines file, or paste data. Format, delimiter, header row and encoding are detected; override them if needed.
Type a Miller verb chain such as filter '$amount > 100' then sort -nr amount then head -n 10, or click a recipe (Convert, Filter, Sort, Stats, Distinct, Pivot, Join) and edit the field names.
Pick the output format (JSON, JSONL, CSV, TSV, Markdown, PPRINT, XTAB) and press Transform. Check the table preview, then Download or Copy the full result.
On the command line: localtools-csv-json-transform run --icsv --ojson 'sort -f name' file.csv, or the full Miller CLI with localtools-csv-json-transform mlr.

faqs.q: Is this real Miller?
faqs.a: Yes. Miller 6.22 is compiled into the executable as a Go library and runs through the same entry points as the mlr binary, so every verb, flag and DSL function works the same. Errors are Miller's own messages.

faqs.q: How big can my files be?
faqs.a: Streaming verbs (convert, filter, cut, put, head) handle files larger than memory: a 200 MB, 7-million-row CSV converted to JSONL in about 10 seconds using about 150 MB. Verbs that need all records at once, such as sort, reshape long-to-wide or percentiles, keep the data in memory (sort on that file used about 4.5 GB).

faqs.q: How do I join two files?
faqs.a: Add the second file in the join box and write FILE2 where its path goes, for example join -j id -f FILE2. The second file can be in a different format (a TSV joined to a CSV works); unpaired records can be kept with --ul / --ur.

faqs.q: My CSV uses semicolons, has a BOM, or came from Excel in Latin-1. Will it work?
faqs.a: Yes. Comma, semicolon, pipe and tab delimiters are detected, a UTF-8 BOM is skipped, UTF-16 files (by BOM) and non-UTF-8 files (read as Windows-1252) are converted to UTF-8. Rows with too few or too many cells are accepted unless you untick Allow ragged rows.

faqs.q: Does my data leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. The tool listens on 127.0.0.1 only, uploads go to a temp folder that is deleted after each request, the page loads nothing from the internet, and shell commands from the Miller DSL are disabled in the web UI.

tools.name: Dataset Profiler
tools.description: Profile CSV, Parquet and JSON datasets (types, nulls, distributions) and detect schema and value drift between two files.
tools.engine: DuckDB 1.5.6 (official CLI, bundled): SUMMARIZE plus exact SQL counts, histograms, patterns and drift
tools.engine_reason: DuckDB reads CSV, JSON and Parquet natively with full-file type inference and profiles millions of rows in seconds. The official CLI runs as a sandboxed sidecar, so the tool works offline on every OS without cgo.
tools.release_notes: Fixes: big-integer CSV columns use DuckDB header names (BOM, padded, duplicate and case-colliding headers work); approximate quantiles stay within min/max; Markdown/HTML exports include NaN/Inf counts; faster on wide files.

howto: Run localtools-dataset-profiler (or open Dataset Profiler from your app menu); it opens in your browser.
Drop a CSV, TSV, JSON/JSONL or Parquet file. Optionally drop a second file to compare against.

Press Profile datasets. Each column shows its inferred type, exact null and distinct counts, min/max/mean/stddev, approximate quartiles, top values, a histogram (numbers) or patterns and formats (text), plus sample rows.
With two files, the drift table lists added, removed and type-changed columns, a total-variation score per column and the change in null share.

Download the report as JSON, Markdown, HTML or a CSV table. From a terminal: localtools-dataset-profiler profile data.csv --json, or localtools-dataset-profiler drift before.csv after.parquet --html > drift.html.

faqs.q: Which numbers are exact?
faqs.a: Row, null and distinct counts, top-value counts, min/max and format matches are exact over the whole file. Quartiles come from DuckDB SUMMARIZE and are approximate; mean, standard deviation and drift scores use floating point. Large integers are sent as strings, so 9007199254740993 stays exact.

faqs.q: How big can a file be?
faqs.a: Up to 64 MiB, 2 million rows and 256 columns per file, with a 120-second deadline per profile. Larger or deeper inputs are refused with a clear message instead of hanging.

faqs.q: What does the drift score mean?
faqs.a: Total variation distance between the two value-frequency distributions of a column, including nulls: 0 means identical frequencies, 1 means no value in common. It measures how much the distribution moved, not statistical significance, and does not match rows by key.

faqs.q: Does my data leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Files are profiled by a bundled DuckDB that is locked to a per-request temporary folder with network access and extension loading disabled; the folder is deleted after each profile.

faqs.q: How are patterns and formats detected?
faqs.a: Text values are reduced to shapes (A for upper case, a for lower case, 9 for digits) and the five most common shapes are listed. Values that fully match email, URL, UUID, ISO date, IPv4, integer or decimal patterns are counted exactly.

tools.name: JSON to Excel
tools.description: Convert JSON or JSONL into formatted .xlsx workbooks with typed columns and multiple sheets.
tools.engine_reason: excelize is the most complete pure-Go .xlsx writer (styles, tables, conditional formats, charts, streaming): one static binary, no Office or runtime needed.
tools.release_notes: - Table names must be unique across the workbook (ignoring case); duplicates are rejected, and unnamed tables get generated names that avoid yours. - A table with "header": false is an error (Excel tables need a header row) instead of being dropped silently. - Row counts for spec sheets without a header are correct. - In an object of arrays, empty arrays are skipped with a warning instead of failing the whole input.

howto: Run localtools-json-to-excel (or open JSON to Excel from your app menu); it opens in your browser.
Paste JSON or drop a .json / .jsonl file. Arrays, JSON Lines and objects of arrays (one sheet per key) are detected automatically.
Optionally set the sheet name or switch off the frozen header, then press Convert.
Check the preview of the first rows and press Download .xlsx.
For scripts: localtools-json-to-excel convert in.json -o out.xlsx, or pipe JSON through stdin.

faqs.q: Are dates and numbers real Excel values or text?
faqs.a: Real values. JSON numbers and booleans become Excel numbers and booleans, and ISO dates (2024-03-01) and datetimes (2024-03-01T14:30:00Z) become Excel dates with a date format, so sorting, filters and formulas work. Integers longer than 15 digits stay text so Excel does not round them.

faqs.q: What happens to nested objects and arrays?
faqs.a: Nested objects are flattened into dotted columns such as customer.address.city. Arrays of plain values go into one cell as a comma-separated list; arrays of objects are kept as compact JSON in one cell.

faqs.q: How big a file can it handle?
faqs.a: Up to Excel's limit of 1,048,575 data rows per sheet. 100,000 rows convert in a few seconds, and nothing is uploaded: the conversion runs on your machine.

faqs.q: Can I control formats, formulas and charts?
faqs.a: Yes, with spec mode: send {"sheets": [...]} with typed columns, number formats, styles, merged cells, formulas, conditional formatting, Excel tables, charts and images. The format is documented in SPEC.md, linked from the README and the UI.

faqs.q: Can a value like =SUM(A1:A9) in my data run as a formula?
faqs.a: No. In data mode every string is written as text, so values starting with = cannot become formulas. Formulas only come from spec mode, where you declare them explicitly.

tools.name: Excel Diff
tools.description: Compare two Excel or CSV files cell by cell: values, formulas, formats, inserted rows and columns, sheets and named ranges.
tools.engine: Go: streaming xlsx reader + Myers row/column alignment; excelize for the annotated workbook
tools.engine_reason: A streaming reader shows every value exactly as stored (comparison uses the stored double, like Excel) and handles a million cells in seconds; Myers O(ND) alignment, with per-column alignment when a column changed in every row, finds inserted and deleted rows and columns; excelize writes B back with the changes highlighted.
tools.release_notes:
- Rows align when one column changed in every row plus inserted rows (correct, under a second); large blocks are paired by position.
- Annotated workbook works without a stylesheet and with openpyxl/pandas colours; a failed -o leaves no partial file.
- Less re-save noise (default validation attributes, empty inline strings, built-in formats, quoted sheet names in names).
- Date-system changes have their own label; one file argument exits 2.

howto: Run localtools-excel-diff (or open Excel Diff from your app menu); it opens in your browser.
Drop the original workbook as A and the changed one as B (.xlsx, .xlsm or .csv).
Optionally ignore whitespace, case, number formats or formulas, or give key columns (e.g. A) to match rows by ID, then press Compare.
Pick a sheet and step through the highlighted changes with Previous/Next change; click a cell to see old and new value, formula and format.
Download the report as JSON or CSV, or an annotated copy of B with changed cells highlighted. From scripts: localtools-excel-diff old.xlsx new.xlsx --json (exit code 1 when different).

faqs.q: Does inserting a row make every cell below it look changed?
faqs.a: No. Rows and columns are aligned first (Myers diff over row hashes, like git diff), so an inserted or deleted row or column is reported once and the cells below are compared with their real counterparts.

faqs.q: Are numbers rounded?
faqs.a: Values are shown and exported exactly as stored in the file, so 12345678901234567890 stays intact. Equality uses the stored double, like Excel, so 0.1 and 0.10000000000000001 count as equal.

faqs.q: My rows were re-sorted. Can it still match them?
faqs.a: Yes: enter one or more key columns (for example A or A,C). Rows are then matched by those values, like a database diff, and only real changes are reported.

faqs.q: What else is compared besides cell values?
faqs.a: Formula text, number formats, optionally cell styles, sheets added/removed/renamed (renames are detected by content), defined names, merged ranges, data validations and comments.

faqs.q: Can it compare a CSV with a workbook, or .ods files?
faqs.a: CSV against CSV or against a workbook works (numbers compare by value). OpenDocument .ods and legacy .xls are not supported; save them as .xlsx first.

tools.name: YAML JSON Query
tools.description: Query and edit YAML, JSON, XML, TOML and INI with yq expressions and apply RFC 6902 JSON Patch, keeping comments.
tools.engine_reason: yq is the de-facto YAML query tool, preserves comments, and handles JSON/XML/TOML/INI as a Go library.
tools.release_notes: Large-input and robustness fixes: the UI/API upload limit is now 16 MB, which reliably fits the 2 GB worker (measured peak heap: 1.0 GB for 16 MB of dense JSON, 1.1 GB for 16 MB of Kubernetes YAML); bigger inputs get a clear "input too large" message. Workers stop when the request is cancelled, when the tool exits, or at their own deadline, and at most two run at once. JSON: nesting deeper than 10000 levels is a clean error, duplicate keys keep the last value, a UTF-8 BOM is accepted. YAML numbers like 0b101, 017, .inf and integers beyond 64 bits convert to JSON/TOML correctly or fail with a clear message. UI: Ctrl+Enter no longer starts a second run while one is in progress.

smoke.expect: replicas: 4 # scaled by HPA in prod

howto: Paste YAML, JSON, TOML, XML, INI, CSV or .properties, or drop the file.
Query mode: write a yq expression such as .spec.template.spec.containers[].image, or .version = "2.0" to edit. Use . with another output format to convert.
Patch mode: paste an RFC 6902 JSON Patch (array) or an RFC 7386 merge patch (object).
Press Run (Ctrl+Enter); copy or download the result. From a terminal: localtools-yaml-json-query eval|convert|patch.

faqs.q: Are YAML comments kept when I edit or patch a file?
faqs.a: Yes. Expressions and patches work on yq's node tree, so comments, anchors, aliases, quoting and key order survive. Blank lines are not preserved (a yq limitation).

faqs.q: Which query syntax does it use?
faqs.a: yq's jq-style syntax by default (select, map, del, with_entries, multi-document selection and more). JMESPath is also available for read-only queries.

faqs.q: Why does a patch refuse to change a path under an alias?
faqs.a: The value is shared through a YAML anchor; changing it there would silently change every other place that uses the anchor. Patch the anchor itself instead.

faqs.q: How do I patch the second document of a multi-document YAML file?
faqs.a: Set the YAML document number to 1 in the UI, or pass --doc 1 on the command line. The other documents are written back unchanged.

faqs.q: Does my data leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs in the local executable on 127.0.0.1; the page loads nothing from the network.

tools.name: OpenAPI Diff
tools.description: Diff two OpenAPI 3 or Swagger specs and list breaking changes with severity.
tools.engine_reason: oasdiff has the most complete OpenAPI breaking-change rule set and is a Go library.
tools.release_notes: Large diffs stay responsive: capped summary in the page, full Markdown/JSON downloaded from the local server; at most 2 comparisons at once (503 when busy); the worker exits with the server.

howto: Drop or paste the old spec under Base and the new spec under Revision (YAML or JSON; OpenAPI 3.0, 3.1 or Swagger 2.0). For multi-file specs, drop a zip of the folder.
Press Compare. Breaking changes and warnings are listed per operation, each with its oasdiff check ID, what clients must do, and the source line.
Tick Show non-breaking for the full changelog, copy the Markdown summary into your PR, or download the JSON.
In CI: localtools-openapi-diff check base.yaml revision.yaml --fail-on breaking --format markdown exits 1 when breaking changes are found.

faqs.q: Which changes count as breaking?
faqs.a: The tool uses oasdiff's rule set (300+ checks). Examples: removed operations, new required parameters, removed enum values in requests, removed or retyped response properties. Every change carries its check ID, so you can look up the exact rule.

faqs.q: Can it diff specs split across several files?
faqs.a: Yes. Local $refs are followed. In the UI, zip each spec folder and drop the zips. On the command line, pass the root files and the referenced files are read from disk. Remote http $refs are refused because the tool stays offline.

faqs.q: Does it support Swagger 2.0?
faqs.a: Yes. Swagger 2.0 documents are converted to OpenAPI 3 with kin-openapi before the diff, so both sides can even use different versions. Swagger 2.0 files that reference other files are not supported.

faqs.q: What exit codes does the check command use?
faqs.a: 0 when nothing reaches the --fail-on level (default breaking), 1 when something does, 2 on errors such as an unreadable or invalid spec.

faqs.q: Are my specs uploaded anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The tool runs on 127.0.0.1, uploads go to a temporary folder that is deleted after each request, and the page makes no network requests.

tools.name: GraphQL Diff
tools.description: Compare two GraphQL schemas and classify breaking, dangerous and safe changes.
tools.engine_reason: GraphQL Inspector is the reference breaking/dangerous/safe detector; schemas are loaded and merged exactly like its CLI, so change lists are identical (tested on GitHub, GitLab, Shopify, SWAPI schemas).
tools.release_notes: Option rules run before simplifyChanges like the CLI (ignore descriptions no longer hides breaking changes); executables keep file:line:col on SDL errors; workers stop with the server or at their deadline; closing the page stops its job; unknown fragments mark only that file invalid; 150k types / 50k changes in ~15 s; per-file remove.

howto: Run localtools-graphql-diff; the page opens at http://127.0.0.1:47112.
Paste or drop the old and new schema (SDL .graphql files or introspection JSON; several files per side are merged).
Optionally drop your client operation files to see which queries the change breaks.
Press Compare, filter by breaking / dangerous / safe, copy the Markdown for your PR or download JSON.
In CI: localtools-graphql-diff old.graphql new.graphql --fail-on breaking (exit 2 on breaking changes).

faqs.q: Are the results the same as graphql-inspector?
faqs.a: Yes. It runs @graphql-inspector/core 8 and loads schemas and applies rules in the same order as the graphql-inspector CLI. On GitHub, GitLab, Saleor, Shopify and SWAPI schema histories, with every option combination, the lists are identical.

faqs.q: What is the difference between breaking and dangerous?
faqs.a: Breaking changes make existing valid operations fail (removed fields, changed types, new required arguments). Dangerous changes keep operations valid but can change behaviour (new enum values, changed default values, new union members).

faqs.q: Can it use an introspection result instead of SDL?
faqs.a: Yes: a JSON file with __schema or data.__schema works on either side, and can be compared with an SDL file.

faqs.q: How big can schemas be?
faqs.a: Up to 32 MB per side and 200,000 types; 150,000 types with 50,000 breaking changes compare in about 15 seconds. Each comparison runs in its own worker with a 60 s limit.

faqs.q: Does anything get uploaded?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs in the local program on 127.0.0.1 with no network requests.

tools.name: GitHub Actions Linter
tools.description: Lint GitHub Actions workflows and composite actions for errors and security issues (script injection, permissions, unpinned actions) with a fix per finding.
tools.engine_reason: actionlint validates workflow syntax and expression types with bundled action metadata; the checksum-pinned zizmor sidecar adds dedicated offline security audits. Both engines feed one local report without remote fetching.
tools.release_notes: No temp-file leaks on cancelled jobs, discovery before limits (1,000 files / 16 MiB), one-run zizmor batches, real-world action.yml inputs accepted, engine failure fails --fail-on, review minors.

howto: Open GitHub Actions Linter (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47113).
Paste a workflow or action.yml, drop files or a .zip, or choose a repository folder: .github/workflows/* and action.yml files are picked up.
Press Lint workflows: actionlint correctness checks and offline zizmor security audits give one list with file:line:column, severity, explanation and a fix snippet.
Ignore rules you accept (field or per-finding button), then download JSON, SARIF or Markdown.
In CI: localtools-github-actions-linter check . --format sarif --fail-on warn > actions.sarif (exit 2 when warnings or errors remain).

faqs.q: Does it contact GitHub or upload my workflow?
faqs.a: No. Both engines run locally. zizmor always runs with --offline --no-config and without your GitHub credentials, so online audits (known-vulnerable-actions, impostor-commit, ref-confusion, stale-action-refs) are not included.

faqs.q: What checks are included?
faqs.a: actionlint 1.7.12 checks syntax, expressions and contexts, needs, matrix, runner labels and popular-action inputs; zizmor 1.31.1 adds template injection, unpinned actions, excessive permissions, dangerous triggers, credential persistence, cache poisoning and more. Composite action.yml files are audited by zizmor and checked against actionlint's action schema.

faqs.q: How do I silence a finding?
faqs.a: Use --ignore rule-id (or the UI field and per-finding button), --ignore-regex for actionlint messages, or a # zizmor: ignore[rule] comment on the reported line.

faqs.q: Can it fail CI or feed GitHub code scanning?
faqs.a: Yes. --fail-on error|warn|info exits with code 2 when such findings exist, and --format sarif writes SARIF 2.1.0.

faqs.q: Does it fix or pin actions for me?
faqs.a: No. Every finding has a fix snippet to apply by hand. Offline it cannot look up commit SHAs, so it tells you where to find the SHA and never invents one.

tools.name: Kubernetes Manifest Checker
tools.description: Score Kubernetes YAML and Helm-rendered manifests for production readiness and security, with a fix snippet per finding.
tools.engine: Go + kube-score library + pod security checks
tools.engine_reason: kube-score (Go, MIT) checks single objects and cross-object relationships; localtools adds a documented subset of versioned Pod Security Standards checks, API removals and duplicate detection.
tools.release_notes: Fix nested-zip memory growth and enforce 16 MiB report limits for every format; add a 2,000-container limit, baseline/restricted capability allowlists, host ports, sysctls, SELinux, procMount and AppArmor checks; decode UTF-16, normalize pod boolean spellings, improve field/archive errors and remove duplicate API findings and kit demo pages.

howto: Open Kubernetes Manifest Checker (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47114).
Paste rendered multi-document YAML, or drop files/a zip. Limits: 8 MiB, 500 resources, 2,000 containers; expand YAML aliases and nested archives first.
Pick the Kubernetes version you deploy to, so removed and deprecated apiVersions are flagged correctly.
Press Check manifests: every object gets a score and grade, every finding a severity, file and line, explanation and YAML fix snippet.
Ignore checks you accept with the field or the per-finding button, then download JSON, SARIF or Markdown.
In CI: localtools-k8s-manifest-checker check ./manifests --k8s-version 1.31 --format sarif --fail-on error > report.sarif

faqs.q: Does it need access to my cluster?
faqs.a: No. It checks manifest files offline and never contacts an API server, so it works on rendered charts before anything is deployed.

faqs.q: Which checks run?
faqs.a: kube-score 1.20.0 plus localtools checks for host namespaces/paths/ports, capabilities, privilege escalation, seccomp, sysctls, SELinux, procMount and AppArmor, plus target-version API removals and duplicates. These are a documented subset of Pod Security Standards, not full admission/schema validation. Inputs allow 8 MiB, 500 resources and 2,000 total containers; each report format is capped at 16 MiB.

faqs.q: Can I use it with Helm or Kustomize?
faqs.a: Yes. Render first and pipe the output: helm template my ./chart | localtools-k8s-manifest-checker check -. It does not run Helm or Kustomize itself.

faqs.q: How do I silence a check?
faqs.a: Use --ignore id1,id2 (or the Ignore field in the UI) for everything, or annotate one object with kube-score/ignore: id1,id2. Ignored checks do not count towards the score.

faqs.q: Can it fail a CI build or show results in GitHub?
faqs.a: Yes. --fail-on error (or warn/info) exits with code 2 when such findings exist, and --format sarif produces SARIF 2.1.0 for GitHub code scanning.

tools.name: Terraform Plan Viewer
tools.description: Review terraform or OpenTofu plan JSON offline: destructive changes first, attribute diffs, blast radius, drift and risk flags.
tools.engine_reason: terraform-json is HashiCorp's typed Go model of terraform show -json output; decoded with json.Number so values stay exact. OpenTofu emits the same format.
tools.release_notes: The sensitive-equality guard no longer hides ordinary values: only marked strings of 8+ bytes (any length within the same resource), never bools, numbers or short strings; hidden values are labelled (matches a sensitive value). Import IDs and check messages pass through the guard. Untraced blast radii past the graph limit say unknown.

smoke.expect: Plan: 1 to import, 7 to add, 1 to change, 7 to destroy.

howto: Open Terraform Plan Viewer (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47115).
Save your plan as JSON: terraform plan -out plan.out, then terraform show -json plan.out > plan.json (tofu works the same).
Drop plan.json or paste it, then press Analyze plan.
Review destructive changes first, open a resource for its attribute diff and blast radius, and check the Drift, Outputs and Checks tabs.
Copy the Markdown summary into your pull request, or download the JSON review.
In CI: localtools-terraform-plan-viewer check plan.json --fail-on delete,replace exits 2 when the plan deletes or replaces anything.

faqs.q: Can it read plan.out or the text output of terraform plan?
faqs.a: No. It reads the JSON from terraform show -json plan.out (or tofu show -json). Binary plan files need Terraform and provider schemas, and plan text is meant for people and hides values, so it is rejected with a hint instead of guessed at.

faqs.q: Are sensitive values safe?
faqs.a: Anything marked sensitive, and any structure containing a marked part, is shown only as (sensitive value) in the page, the Markdown, the JSON export and the CLI. As a precaution, an unmarked string equal to a marked one (8+ characters elsewhere in the plan, any length in the same resource) is shown as (matches a sensitive value); this also applies to import IDs and check messages. Plan variables are never echoed. Nothing leaves your machine.

faqs.q: How is the blast radius computed?
faqs.a: From the configuration block in the plan JSON: expression references, depends_on, count/for_each and module inputs and outputs. Each change lists the resources and root outputs downstream of it. References through local values cannot be traced because Terraform omits locals from plan JSON.

faqs.q: Does it work with OpenTofu?
faqs.a: Yes. OpenTofu writes the same plan JSON format. The engine is recognised from provider registry addresses; plans that use only built-in providers are labelled Terraform or OpenTofu, and the plan line then includes forget counts as OpenTofu prints them.

faqs.q: How large a plan can it handle?
faqs.a: Up to 64 MiB of JSON. A 59 MiB plan with 100,000 resources takes about 3 seconds; the page shows 200 resources at a time.

tools.name: Postgres Migration Checker
tools.description: Check PostgreSQL migrations for the lock each statement takes, what it blocks, and a safe rewrite.
tools.engine_reason: postgast calls the real libpg_query parser, so lock and rewrite rules follow a typed PostgreSQL AST instead of regex splits. The abandoned GPL pglast scaffold is not bundled. PyPI has postgast wheels for Windows x64, Linux x64 and macOS ARM64. A plain Intel macOS PyPI install is unavailable: upstream has no Intel wheel, and its published source archive lacks build headers. Use the self-contained Intel Mac ZIP, or the bundled MacIntel postgast wheel with Python 3.13: `pipx install localtools-postgres-migration-checker --python python3.13 --pip-args="--find-links https://github.com/chayprabs/localtools/releases/download/postgres-migration-checker-v1.0.0/postgast-0.2.0-cp313-cp313-macosx_10_13_x86_64.whl"`. That wheel is built unmodified from the upstream v0.2.0 Git tag.
tools.release_notes: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS no longer hides later heavy DDL on a table that may already exist. ALTER TYPE follows the full binary-coercible cast set (text to varchar, xml to text, int4/oid, wider precision); timestamp to timestamptz is flagged as UTC-only. SET (user_catalog_table) takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Flyway files with only non-transactional statements run without a transaction. Placeholder snippets are commented out. UI: unclipped transaction select, padded results.

fields.sql: ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

howto: Install with the one-line script, or pipx install localtools-postgres-migration-checker, then run localtools-postgres-migration-checker.
Paste UTF-8 SQL or choose .sql files in the order they run. A new paste or upload replaces the previous input, and each chosen file can be removed.
Set the target PostgreSQL version (11–18, default 18) and the runner transaction: detect framework markers and explicit BEGIN, wrap each file, or never wrap.
Click Check migration. Each statement shows its lock, what that lock blocks, whether it scans or rewrites the table, and a safer rewrite when the rule has one.
Copy JSON or download JSON, Markdown or SARIF. The page shows 50 statements at a time; the download is the full report.

faqs.q: Does it run the SQL against a database?
faqs.a: No. It parses the text with libpg_query and never opens a connection. The report stays on your machine.

faqs.q: Why does ADD COLUMN age int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 still take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE?
faqs.a: On PostgreSQL 11 and later a constant default does not rewrite the table. ADD COLUMN still takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE until the catalog change commits. That statement is flagged for a missing lock_timeout, not for a rewrite.

faqs.q: Can pipx install it on an Intel Mac?
faqs.a: Not from PyPI alone. Upstream publishes no Intel wheel, and its source archive lacks build headers. Use the Intel Mac ZIP, or Python 3.13 with pipx install localtools-postgres-migration-checker --python python3.13 --pip-args="--find-links https://github.com/chayprabs/localtools/releases/download/postgres-migration-checker-v1.0.0/postgast-0.2.0-cp313-cp313-macosx_10_13_x86_64.whl". That is the bundled MacIntel postgast 0.2.0 wheel, built unmodified from the upstream v0.2.0 Git tag.

faqs.q: Which migration runners does it understand?
faqs.a: goose Up/Down/NO TRANSACTION, dbmate up/down and transaction:false, Liquibase formatted SQL changesets and runInTransaction:false, and Flyway V…__…sql or R__…sql filenames. Down sections are omitted. Rails and Django need exported SQL plus the transaction mode you choose.

faqs.q: How large a migration can it check, and what does it skip?
faqs.a: 100 files, 4 MiB of UTF-8 SQL, 5,000 statements, a 16 MiB report, 30 seconds, and two checks at a time. Larger input is rejected. Function bodies, DO blocks, dynamic SQL, views, triggers and the live schema are not modelled. Locks are static estimates, not measurements from a running database.

tools.name: SQL Formatter
tools.description: Format and lint SQL in any major dialect with sqlfluff, including auto-fix.
tools.engine_reason: sqlfluff is the most complete open-source SQL linter with real auto-fix across dialects; sqlglot adds dialect-to-dialect transpiling, which sqlfluff cannot do.
tools.release_notes: 1.0.1: a cancelled run no longer blocks the next one, so the latest SQL is what gets linted, fixed or transpiled. Unsupported placeholders and unknown rules error clearly, in-place writes stay atomic, diffs apply without a final newline, and the Raw templater plus non-ligature code font are in the release.

howto: Paste SQL or drop one or more .sql files.
Pick the dialect (Postgres, MySQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, T-SQL, DuckDB and 22 more); optionally choose rules, a templater (Jinja or placeholders) or upload your .sqlfluff / pyproject.toml.
Press Lint to see every violation with line, column, rule code and a link to the rule docs.
Switch to Fix (or press Fix all) to get the fixed SQL with a diff; copy or download it.
Use Transpile to convert a query between dialects, e.g. T-SQL to Postgres.

faqs.q: Are the results the same as the sqlfluff CLI?
faqs.a: Yes. It runs sqlfluff 4 with your dialect and config, and the tests check that lint and fix output equal the sqlfluff CLI on TPC-H, dbt and GitLab SQL.

faqs.q: Can I use my existing .sqlfluff config?
faqs.a: Yes, upload .sqlfluff, setup.cfg, tox.ini or pyproject.toml. It is parsed, never executed: library paths, macro paths and the python/dbt templaters are ignored and listed.

faqs.q: Does it support dbt models?
faqs.a: Use the Jinja templater: it provides dbt's ref, source and config builtins, and fixes are applied to your template source. The full dbt templater (which needs a database connection) is not included.

faqs.q: How big can the SQL be?
faqs.a: The web UI takes up to 512 KB and about 2,000 statements per run, with a 120 second deadline because sqlfluff is thorough but slow. The command line has no limits.

faqs.q: Does my SQL leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs locally on 127.0.0.1; there is no network access or telemetry.

tools.name: Grok Debugger
tools.description: Test grok patterns against log lines with the full Logstash pattern library and highlighted matches.
tools.engine: Own grok compiler on Go RE2 + official Logstash pattern sets (ECS v1 and legacy)
tools.engine_reason: Embeds the unmodified logstash-patterns-core files, so field names match Logstash 8; RE2 is linear-time, so no pattern can hang. Existing Go grok libraries ship their own rewritten legacy-only pattern copies.
tools.release_notes: Match, Suggest and Export share isolated workers, compilation limits, deadlines and cancellation. Uploads are removable and newer pasted input wins; table columns include every row and repeated capture values. Dark legends and API errors are corrected; zips include upstream pattern licenses.

howto: Paste log lines or drop a log file (up to 8 MB in the UI; the CLI has no limit).
Enter one or more grok patterns, one per line; they are tried in order and the first match wins. Browse the Logstash pattern library to insert %{NAME} references, or press "Suggest from first line".
Press Match (Ctrl+Enter): every captured field is color-highlighted in its line; the Table and JSON tabs show the extracted fields and the nested event.
Open Export to get a Logstash filter, Elasticsearch ingest pipeline, Vector VRL or Fluent Bit parser. From a terminal: localtools-grok-debugger match --pattern ... file.log --json.

faqs.q: Does it behave exactly like Logstash?
faqs.a: It uses the same official pattern files (ECS v1 by default, legacy optional) and Logstash rules for named captures, empty captures and int/float hints. The regex engine is Go RE2 instead of Oniguruma: atomic groups and possessive quantifiers are relaxed, and lookarounds or backreferences in your own patterns give an error with the column.

faqs.q: How does pattern suggestion work?
faqs.a: A deterministic tokenizer recognizes timestamps, IPs, HTTP request lines, log levels, paths, numbers, key=value pairs and prog[pid], then names the fields. The suggestion is matched against the line before it is shown. No AI or network is involved.

faqs.q: Can a slow pattern freeze it?
faqs.a: The UI/API allow 50 patterns of 16 KB each, expanding to 1 MB of regex in total. Match, Suggest and Export share two isolated worker slots, each killed after 15 seconds or on disconnect. Matching returns partial results after 10 seconds, with timing and slow-pattern warnings.

faqs.q: Are the Vector and Fluent Bit exports tested?
faqs.a: Yes. CI runs the generated configs through the real vector and fluent-bit binaries and checks they extract the same fields as the tool.

faqs.q: Can I add my own patterns?
faqs.a: Yes, under Custom patterns (or --custom FILE): one NAME regex per line, like a Logstash patterns_dir file. They override library patterns with the same name.

tools.name: CLI Output to JSON
tools.description: Convert command output (ls, ps, netstat, dig, network device show commands) into JSON with jc and TextFSM.
tools.engine_reason: jc 1.26.0 parses 243 OS commands; TextFSM 2.1.0 with ntc-templates 9.3.0 adds 969 indexed network-device templates. Both are pinned in the portable CPython zip and run offline, with no command execution.
tools.release_notes: macOS parses again. Setting the 768 MiB address-space cap raised on macOS and the worker exited before writing a result, so POST /api/parse returned 422. That call is ignored when the OS refuses it. Linux still applies the cap.

fields.input:
Filesystem     1K-blocks     Used Available Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        1000000    50000    950000   5% /

howto: Paste UTF-8 command output, or choose one text file. The newest input replaces the other.
Search the catalog and select a parser. jc ids are command names such as df; network templates start with ntc/.
Optional: type a command hint and a network platform, then press Suggest parsers. Choose a candidate yourself; nothing is selected for you.
Choose JSON, compact JSON, JSON Lines, or CSV, then press Convert.
Read the records and notes. Copy and Download keep the full result; the on-screen preview stops at 128 KiB of characters.

faqs.q: Does this run the command or connect to the device?
faqs.a: No. It only parses text you paste or upload. The command hint is a lookup string, never executed, and the tool makes no network connections.

faqs.q: Will Suggest parsers pick the right one?
faqs.a: No. Suggestions come from jc's command index, the ntc-templates command index, or a few familiar headers. You have to select a parser. Extracting zero records does not prove the text matched.

faqs.q: Which network-device templates are included?
faqs.a: The 969 indexed ntc-templates 9.3.0 entries (TextFSM 2.1.0). Custom templates, unindexed templates, and remote device execution are not included.

faqs.q: What are the size limits?
faqs.a: 4 MiB of UTF-8, 100,000 lines, and 65,536 characters on a line. Results stop at 16 MiB. Each parse has a 15-second deadline, and only two parser jobs run at once.

faqs.q: Why can fields be missing or typed differently from the text?
faqs.a: jc and TextFSM follow their own rules: unmatched lines can be ignored, duplicate keys can collapse, and values can be inferred. Dates use the machine's timezone, the same way jc does. Compare the JSON with the original output.

tools.name: HTML Extractor
tools.description: Extract data from HTML pages with CSS selectors into JSON or CSV.
tools.engine_reason: Cascadia selectors over the x/net/html HTML5 parser provide CSS matching, entity decoding and browser-style HTML repair in one pure-Go executable; no browser runtime or goquery dependency is needed.
tools.release_notes: Blank meta charset values are ignored instead of failing the page; internal failures report as internal errors; attribute flags without a space parse; case-insensitive enumerated attribute values apply only to HTML elements, as in Chromium.

howto: Open HTML Extractor (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47120).
Paste HTML or choose a saved .html file.
Enter a row selector, e.g. article or tr: one result row per match.
Edit the field map: a name, a CSS selector inside the row, and optionally an attribute such as href.
Press Extract, then copy or download the JSON or CSV.
From a terminal: localtools-html-extractor extract --rows article --fields fields.json --format csv page.html > out.csv

faqs.q: Can it fetch a live URL or run the page's JavaScript?
faqs.a: No. It works on HTML you paste or save, entirely offline. Save the page from your browser (or with curl) first; content built by JavaScript must be saved after it has rendered.

faqs.q: Which CSS selectors are supported?
faqs.a: The Cascadia selector set used by goquery: type, class, id, attribute, combinators, :nth-child, :not, :has, :contains and more. An unsupported selector is reported as an error instead of silently matching nothing.

faqs.q: What happens with broken HTML?
faqs.a: It is repaired the way browsers do, using Go's HTML5 parser, so unclosed tags and missing tbody elements behave as in a browser. Declared legacy encodings such as windows-1252 or Shift_JIS are decoded.

faqs.q: Will large numeric IDs be rounded?
faqs.a: No. Every value is returned as a string, so an ID like 9007199254740993 stays exact in both JSON and CSV.

faqs.q: How big can the input be?
faqs.a: Up to 4 MiB of HTML, 5,000 rows and 20 fields per run, with a 10-second limit. Larger inputs are rejected with a clear message instead of hanging.

tools.name: SSL Checker
tools.description: Check a domain's TLS certificate chain, expiry, supported protocols, DNSSEC and CAA records.
tools.engine: Go crypto/tls + crypto/x509 + miekg/dns, Mozilla roots from golang.org/x/crypto/x509roots
tools.engine_reason: Go's TLS stack and verifier give real handshakes and chain checks without OpenSSL; miekg/dns sets DO/AD/CD bits for DNSSEC; the Go team's CCADB-generated Mozilla bundle keeps distrust-after constraints.
tools.release_notes: Weak ciphers are probed with raw ClientHellos per class (NULL/export, RC4, 3DES, RSA key exchange, CBC), matching what servers really accept; CBC and RSA key exchange are informational. DNS lookup failures and NXDOMAIN are reported as such, errors are one human line, oversized/JSON API bodies get 413/415, inspect accepts flags after the file, UI spacing fixed.

howto: Enter one or more hosts, one per line: example.com, host:port or an https:// URL (up to 20 per check; internal and loopback hosts work).
Pick a DNS resolver (system, Cloudflare, Google or Quad9) and press Check. Each host gets a card with pass, warn, fail and info lines.
Open the chain, protocol and DNS folds for every certificate field, fingerprints, per-version support and records; Download JSON saves the full report.
Offline: switch to Inspect certificate and drop a PEM, DER or .p7b file (or paste PEM) to inspect and verify it without network.
In CI: localtools-ssl-checker check example.com --json exits 2 when any check fails.

faqs.q: Why do the system and Mozilla results differ?
faqs.a: They are two root stores. On Windows and macOS the system verifier can download a missing intermediate, so a server with an incomplete chain passes there but fails the Mozilla check, like Firefox. The Mozilla roots are the Go team's CCADB-generated bundle embedded in the binary, including distrust-after dates.

faqs.q: Which hosts does it connect to?
faqs.a: Only the hosts you type and the DNS resolver you pick. Private and loopback addresses are allowed on purpose, so you can check internal certificates. The local API only accepts requests from its own page.

faqs.q: How is DNSSEC decided?
faqs.a: It asks the resolver with the DNSSEC OK and AD bits. AD set means secure. SERVFAIL that goes away with checking disabled means bogus. Signatures without AD mean the resolver does not validate, so choose Cloudflare, Google or Quad9.

faqs.q: Does it list every cipher suite the server accepts?
faqs.a: No. It sends one raw ClientHello per weak class (NULL/export, RC4, 3DES, RSA key exchange, CBC) and reports the suite the server picks in each, so it sees suites Go itself cannot negotiate. RC4 and NULL fail, 3DES warns, RSA key exchange and CBC are info. STARTTLS is not included.

faqs.q: What are the limits?
faqs.a: 10 seconds per connection and handshake, 25 seconds per host, 20 hosts per UI check (500 in the CLI), two checks at a time. Offline input is up to 4 MiB and 500 certificates.

tools.name: Archive Inspector
tools.description: List and inspect nested zip, tar, 7z, rar, gz, xz and zst archives and flag zip bombs and path traversal.
tools.engine_reason: Pure Go: one static binary reads zip/tar/7z/rar and every compression layer through one streaming API, with direct zip offsets for overlap-bomb detection; no cgo libarchive or bundled 7-Zip.
tools.release_notes: Review fixes: linear name checks on very deep paths, CP437 zip names and index-based entry addressing, stricter Windows-safe extraction (invalid characters, NUL .txt, CONIN$, COM¹), mixed-script-only homoglyph warnings, self-extracting zips, nameless/empty 7z, empty files rejected, DOS zip times without a zone.

howto: Open Archive Inspector (it starts at http://127.0.0.1:47122).
Choose an archive: zip, jar, apk, docx, whl, tar, tgz, tar.xz, gz, zst, 7z or rar (up to 512 MiB).
Press Inspect: read the safety verdict and findings, then browse every entry, including archives nested inside it.
Use Preview, SHA-256 or Download on any file without extracting the archive; add a second archive to see what changed.
From a terminal: localtools-archive-inspector check upload.zip (exit code 2 when unsafe), or extract upload.zip -o out for a safe extraction.

faqs.q: Does it extract the archive to disk?
faqs.a: No. Listing, previews and hashes read entries straight from the archive. Nested archives are copied to a temporary file only to be opened, and that file is deleted afterwards. Extraction happens only when you run the extract command.

faqs.q: Which zip bombs does it detect?
faqs.a: Extreme compression ratios, archives that declare far more data than their size (like the passwordless 42.zip, whose nested layers expand to petabytes), overlapping entries that reuse the same compressed data (David Fifield's zbsm.zip), and archives that contain themselves (r.zip). Reading stops after 1 GiB of decompressed data in any case. Password-protected archives, such as the original 42.zip, are listed and flagged as encrypted, but their contents cannot be checked.

faqs.q: What makes an entry unsafe?
faqs.a: Paths with .., absolute paths or drive letters (zip slip), symlinks or hard links pointing outside the archive, entries written through a symlink, Unicode direction-override characters, executables disguised as documents or with double extensions, plus warnings for duplicates, case collisions, setuid bits and encrypted entries.

faqs.q: Can it open password-protected archives?
faqs.a: No. Encrypted entries and archives are listed where the format allows and flagged as encrypted, but never decrypted.

faqs.q: Is the extract command safe to use on untrusted archives?
faqs.a: It writes only regular files and directories into a new or empty folder, refuses traversal paths, links, device files and Windows device names, never overwrites files and stops at 1 GiB or 20,000 entries (adjustable). Every refused entry is listed.

tools.name: Video Thumbnail Generator
tools.description: Generate thumbnails, frame grids and contact sheets from video files with ffmpeg.
tools.engine: ffmpeg + ffprobe 9.0.2 (bundled: BtbN gpl-shared on Windows/Linux, Martin Riedl static builds on macOS)
tools.engine_reason: ffmpeg decodes practically every codec and container, seeks frame-accurately and tone-maps HDR with zscale; it runs as a killable child process, so the tool works offline on every OS with no system install.
tools.release_notes: First release: frames at a timestamp with a scrubbing preview, evenly spaced frames, scene-change picks, contact sheets and animated GIF/WebP previews, with an ffprobe info panel. HDR tone mapping, rotation and deinterlacing applied. Bundles unmodified ffmpeg 9.0.2 (GPL); its sources are attached to the release.

howto: Run localtools-video-thumbnail-generator (or open Video Thumbnail Generator from your app menu); it opens in your browser.
Drop a video (up to 4 GiB, any format ffmpeg reads). The info panel lists duration, codecs, resolution, frame rate, rotation, colour/HDR details and every stream.
Drag the scrubber to preview any moment, or pick a mode: single frame, evenly spaced frames, scene changes, contact sheet or animated GIF/WebP.
Choose PNG, JPEG or WebP, a width and quality, then press Generate. Download each image or all of them as a zip.
From a terminal: localtools-video-thumbnail-generator grid video.mp4 --cols 4 --rows 4 -o sheet.jpg, frame video.mp4 --at 00:01:23, or info video.mp4 --json.

faqs.q: Does my video leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. The browser sends it to the tool on 127.0.0.1, which keeps it in a temporary folder for this session, runs the bundled ffmpeg on it with network protocols disabled, and deletes the folder when you remove the video, after 30 idle minutes, or when the tool exits.

faqs.q: Which formats work?
faqs.a: Anything the bundled ffmpeg 9.0.2 can decode: MP4, MOV, MKV, WebM, AVI, MPEG-TS, raw H.264/HEVC streams and more, with H.264, HEVC, AV1, VP9, ProRes and other codecs. Playlists that point at other files or URLs (HLS, concat, DASH) are refused.

faqs.q: Are HDR and phone videos handled?
faqs.a: Yes. HDR10 and HLG are tone-mapped to SDR (zscale + hable) unless you turn it off, rotation metadata and non-square pixels are applied, and interlaced video is deinterlaced with bwdif.

faqs.q: How exact are the timestamps?
faqs.a: Frames are taken with an accurate seek: the tests compare them with ffmpeg's own frame at the same time (PSNR above 38 dB). Evenly spaced frames sit at the middle of equal slices of the video; scene picks come from ffmpeg's scene score.

faqs.q: What are the limits?
faqs.a: 4 GiB per upload (the CLI has none), 100 frames per job, 8K per image, 50 megapixels per contact sheet, 15 seconds per animation and 180 seconds per job. Bigger requests are refused with a clear message instead of hanging.

tools.name: Loudness Normalizer
tools.description: Normalize audio loudness to EBU R128 / LUFS targets with two-pass ffmpeg loudnorm.
tools.engine: ffmpeg + ffprobe 9.0.2, EBU R128 ebur128 + two-pass loudnorm (bundled)
tools.engine_reason: ffmpeg supplies real EBU R128 measurement and two-pass loudnorm with a true-peak limiter; SHA256-pinned sidecars run offline as killable children on every supported OS.
tools.release_notes: Fix quiet-audio true/sample-peak precision and cap peak-mode gain at +60 dB. Remeasure up to three encodes, use a final oversampled limiter for transient overshoot, and retain the best attempt. Web deadlines scale with duration; CLI has no time limit. Keep narrow-screen file values/actions visible. Document the conservative EBU case 16 engine limit and only shipped architectures.

howto: Run localtools-loudness-normalizer or open Loudness Normalizer from your app menu.
Drop audio or video files to measure LUFS, loudness range and true peak, and select a row for its loudness graph.
Choose a platform preset or custom target, or use peak normalization or a fixed gain. Choose the output format and bitrate when needed.
Press Normalize all, inspect before/after values and processing notes, then download audio individually or as one ZIP. Copy or download the selected report.
CLI: localtools-loudness-normalizer measure song.flac --json; localtools-loudness-normalizer normalize song.flac --preset ebu -o normalized.flac.

faqs.q: Does audio leave my computer?
faqs.a: No. The browser uploads to the tool on 127.0.0.1 and the bundled ffmpeg works offline. Uploads are removed when released, after 30 idle minutes, or at shutdown; stale crash folders are swept on restart.

faqs.q: Does normalization change the dynamics?
faqs.a: A linear gain preserves dynamics whenever the true-peak ceiling allows. Otherwise loudnorm compresses and limits the audio, and the report identifies dynamic mode. Choose a loudness range target only when compression is wanted.

faqs.q: Which formats and video files work?
faqs.a: ffmpeg reads WAV, FLAC, MP3, AAC, Opus, Ogg and audio tracks in MP4, MOV, MKV and other local media. Same-as-source keeps compatible video, other audio tracks, subtitles, cover art and tags; only the first audio track is normalized. Explicit output formats extract audio.

faqs.q: Why can the result differ from the target?
faqs.a: Very short or dynamic audio and lossy encoding can shift loudness or true peak. Each output is re-measured; peak overshoot triggers up to three attempts with less gain or an oversampled limiter, and the best attempt is kept. Remaining deviations are reported. Peak mode refuses more than +60 dB gain. FFmpeg conservatively over-reads the EBU Tech 3341 case 16 true peak (-5.4 instead of -6.0 dBTP).

faqs.q: What are the limits?
faqs.a: 2 GiB and 6 hours per upload, 20 retained files, two jobs at a time, 600 seconds plus 30 seconds per minute of audio per job, up to 8 channels at 384 kHz. The CLI has no upload size, duration or time cap. Silence and audio shorter than 0.4 seconds cannot be LUFS normalized; fixed gain remains available.

tools.name: Subtitle Converter
tools.description: Convert, inspect and re-time subtitles; extract, add or burn captions into video.
tools.engine_reason: Go preserves millisecond timings and raw ASS/WebVTT payloads for timing edits; pinned ffmpeg handles container tracks and libass burn-in as a separate process.
tools.release_notes: Fixes: burn --override-style on ASS files positions top/middle/bottom and sizes text in video pixels; numeric arrow dialogue kept as text; TMPlayer named as unsupported; Baltic windows-1257 detected, more UI encodings, short Western text stays windows-1252; web output limit measures the text.

howto: Choose a subtitle file or paste SRT, WebVTT, ASS/SSA, TTML/DFXP, SBV or MicroDVD text.
Select an output format. Inspect ambiguous encodings before converting.
Optionally shift timing, change frame rates, sync two points or apply cleanup; review the findings.
Run Convert and copy or download the complete UTF-8 result. Merge and split are also available.
For video, select Extract, Add track or Burn, choose a local video, wait for inspection, then run. MKV retains ASS; MP4 soft subtitles lose ASS styling.

faqs.q: Which subtitle formats are supported?
faqs.a: Read SRT, WebVTT, ASS/SSA, TTML/DFXP, SBV/SubViewer and MicroDVD. Write those formats or a plain transcript. MicroDVD needs the video frame rate. TTML sequential containers and timed spans are refused.

faqs.q: Will every style and layout survive conversion?
faqs.a: Basic text styling translates where supported. Fonts, exact layout, animation, karaoke, ruby and metadata can be lost; ASS rounds to centiseconds. Staying in ASS/WebVTT preserves raw cue payloads. MP4 soft subtitles use mov_text.

faqs.q: Can it extract image subtitles or transcribe speech?
faqs.a: It extracts text subtitle tracks. PGS/VobSub image tracks require OCR, which is not included. Speech transcription, translation and online subtitle search are not included.

faqs.q: What are the limits?
faqs.a: 16 MiB per subtitle, 32 MiB per web request, 100,000 cues, 256 KiB per line and 1 MiB per decoded cue. Web subtitles have a 30-second processing deadline. Video uploads are limited to 4 GiB and jobs to three hours; two jobs per category run at once.

faqs.q: How do video burn-in and privacy work?
faqs.a: All work stays on this computer without network access. Burn-in re-encodes to 8-bit H.264; HDR/interlaced inputs are refused. Go Latin fonts are bundled; other scripts/custom fonts depend on installed fonts. Cancellation or server death kills native jobs. Uploads/results expire after 30 minutes idle.

tools.name: EXIF Remover
tools.description: Inspect and remove metadata from JPEG, PNG, TIFF and WebP images; download clean copies and a remaining-tags report.
tools.engine_reason: Mature EXIF/GPS/IPTC/XMP/ICC parsers; tested raster formats, verified cleaned outputs, unmodified portable Windows bundle. macOS/Linux require Perl 5 on PATH.
tools.release_notes: Multi-page TIFF: private and unknown tags removed on every page; warnings deduplicated and capped; per-file report read from the ZIP (no oversized headers); mismatched extensions cleaned as the detected type. Batch image metadata inspection/removal, originals untouched, orientation/color preservation option. JPEG, PNG, TIFF and WebP. 16 files; 32 MiB each; 64 MiB total. Unix requires Perl 5 on PATH. Not a forensic anonymization guarantee.

howto: Install and run localtools-exif-remover. macOS/Linux require Perl 5 on PATH; Windows includes Perl.
Choose up to 16 JPEG, PNG, TIFF or WebP images (32 MiB each, 64 MiB total). Inspect metadata and expand a file to read its tags.
Choose to preserve orientation and color, or remove all deletable metadata. Kept ICC profiles can include author and private values.
Clean the batch, download the ZIP, and review report.json for removed and remaining tags before sharing. Originals are unchanged.

faqs.q: Does this change image quality or my originals?
faqs.a: Originals are untouched. ExifTool copies image pixels without recompression. Removing orientation or color tags can change how viewers display an image; the default preserves those tags.

faqs.q: Which formats can I clean?
faqs.a: JPEG, PNG, TIFF and WebP. RAW, HEIC/AVIF, GIF, PDF, video/audio and Office documents are rejected because their deletion and verification risks differ. TIFF retains required structural tags.

faqs.q: Is every private detail guaranteed gone?
faqs.a: No. The report covers ExifTool-visible tags with capped values. Kept ICC profiles can include author/private values. Unknown or structural data, filenames, visible faces/text and steganography are not anonymized. Inspect remaining tags.

faqs.q: Do I need Perl or an internet connection?
faqs.a: Windows bundles Perl. macOS and Linux require a Perl 5 runtime on PATH; minimal Linux installations may not have one. After installation and that prerequisite, inspection and cleaning run offline.

faqs.q: What are the limits and API output?
faqs.a: Up to 16 files, 32 MiB each and 64 MiB total. Two simultaneous jobs; 60-second deadline. POST multipart file fields to /api/inspect for JSON, or /api/strip with preset=keep or all for a ZIP of cleaned copies and report.json.

tools.name: SVG Optimizer
tools.description: Optimize and minify SVG files with SVGO and export them to PNG.
tools.engine: SVGO 4.1 + allowlist sanitizer (SVGO plugin) + resvg (wasm) for PNG
tools.engine_reason: SVGO is the standard SVG optimizer; resvg-wasm renders PNG accurately without a browser on every OS/arch from one artifact; the sanitizer is a strict allowlist tested against 30 XSS payloads in a live browser.
tools.release_notes: Security: a <style> sheet that fails the check is dropped whole and the final output is sanitized again; only xlink:/xml: prefixes; SMIL may not animate href/style/on*/base. Safe keeps empty elements with ids. Results table fits phone screens.

howto: Run localtools-svg-optimizer; the page opens at http://127.0.0.1:47127.
Drop one or more .svg files (or paste SVG markup).
Pick Safe or Aggressive, plus any toggles: keep viewBox, remove width/height, prefix IDs, multipass, sanitize, PNG width.
Press Optimize to see before/after sizes and side-by-side previews; download one file, its PNG, or all as a zip.
From a terminal: localtools-svg-optimizer optimize icons/ -o out/ --sanitize --png 512

faqs.q: Will the optimized SVG look different, or break my sprite sheet?
faqs.a: Not with the Safe preset: it runs SVGO's preset-default but keeps every id, <symbol> and <defs> entry, so file.svg#icon links and outside CSS keep working, and tests render every sample before and after with resvg (at most 0.5% of pixels may differ). Aggressive also drops unreferenced ids, symbols and defs, <title>/<desc>, and rounds to 2 decimals.

faqs.q: Is it safe to accept SVG uploads after sanitizing?
faqs.a: Sanitize keeps only drawing elements and removes scripts, event handlers, foreignObject, external links, and any CSS that loads something from outside (url(), @import, @font-face, image-set and similar), after decoding CSS escapes the way a browser does. It is tested against 30 SVG XSS payloads and 59 CSS, namespace and SMIL payloads by inlining the result into a live browser page. Still serve user SVGs with a Content-Security-Policy as defence in depth.

faqs.q: Why did removing the viewBox not happen?
faqs.a: SVGO only removes viewBox when width/height make it redundant (same origin and size). With mm units or a different size it keeps it, because removing it would change scaling. Turning on Remove width/height always keeps the viewBox.

faqs.q: Does anything get uploaded?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs in the local program on 127.0.0.1; it makes no network requests.

faqs.q: Why does text in the PNG use a different font?
faqs.a: PNG export uses resvg with your system's common fonts (Arial, Helvetica, DejaVu, Liberation). Fonts not found there fall back to a default. The optimized SVG itself keeps your font settings.

tools.name: OG Image Generator
tools.description: Design and render Open Graph / social card images offline: templates, live preview, code highlighting, batch.
tools.engine_reason: satori lays out HTML/CSS (flex, grid, stylesheets, HarfBuzz shaping) as SVG without a browser; resvg rasterizes it identically on every OS; shiki gives editor-grade code highlighting. All wasm, fonts and emoji are embedded, so nothing is fetched.
tools.release_notes: WebP images decoded (were blank); Connection: close clients get JSON 413/503; nested sections capped; worker replies framed; code card truncation inside the window; human errors for variable fonts and corrupt images; Excel Windows-1252 and semicolon CSV; template picker locks while edited markup is used; stricter URL checks; accurate notices; pinned Bun 1.4.3 builds.

howto: Run localtools-og-image-generator; the page opens at http://127.0.0.1:47128.
Pick a template (blog, docs, launch, repository, quote, code, event, minimal) and a size: OG 1200x630, X 1200x675, square, story or custom.
Edit the fields, upload a logo, avatar, background image or your own font; the preview updates as you type.
Download PNG, JPEG or SVG, or edit the HTML/CSS template in the Markup tab.
For many cards: drop a CSV/JSON in the Batch tab, or run localtools-og-image-generator batch rows.csv --template blog -o cards/.

faqs.q: Does it need a browser or the internet?
faqs.a: No. satori lays out the card and resvg rasterizes it inside the program; fonts, emoji and the code highlighter are embedded. Remote image URLs in templates are rejected and network access is switched off while rendering.

faqs.q: Can I use my own design?
faqs.a: Yes. The Markup tab (or --markup FILE) takes HTML with a <style> sheet and {{field}} placeholders, using satori's CSS subset: flex, grid, gradients, line-clamp, @media on the image size. Errors point to the line and column. The guide is MARKUP.md in this folder.

faqs.q: Which languages and emoji render?
faqs.a: Latin, Greek and Cyrillic with Geist, Inter or JetBrains Mono; Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hebrew and Devanagari fall back to bundled Noto fonts, and emoji use Twemoji. You can also upload .ttf, .otf, .woff or .woff2 fonts. Variable fonts are not supported; upload a static instance.

faqs.q: How many cards can a batch make?
faqs.a: Up to 1,000 rows per batch (500 cards take about 25 s). Columns are field names, a filename column names the files, and image columns refer to uploaded images (or files beside the CSV in the CLI).

faqs.q: What are the limits?
faqs.a: 200 to 4096 px per side, images up to 10 MB / 25 megapixels, up to four fonts of 20 MB, templates up to 512 KB / 5,000 elements, and 20 s per card. Two renders run at once; more wait or get a busy reply.

tools.name: Font Subsetter
tools.description: Subset fonts to the characters you use, instance variable fonts, and convert to WOFF2.
tools.engine_reason: fontTools is the reference font library; pyftsubset and instancer are what font engineers use.
tools.release_notes: Fixes the macOS/Linux launcher when started through the ~/.localtools/bin shim, and update on macOS/Linux.

howto: Drop one or more TTF, OTF, WOFF or WOFF2 fonts.
Tick Unicode presets (Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Vietnamese...) and/or type the exact text you need.
Optionally keep or drop OpenType features, keep hinting, and pin or limit variable axes such as wght=400:700.
Pick WOFF2, WOFF or TTF/OTF and press Subset.
Check the size, glyph count, missing characters and license bits, preview the subset font, then Download and Copy CSS for the @font-face rule.

faqs.q: How much smaller do fonts get?
faqs.a: It depends on how many characters you keep. A Latin-only WOFF2 of a large multi-script font is often 70-95% smaller; keeping only the glyphs of a short headline can shrink a 100 KB font to a few KB.

faqs.q: Will kerning and ligatures still work?
faqs.a: Yes. By default fontTools keeps the standard layout features (kern, liga, calt, mark, locl and more). Choose all to keep every feature, none to drop them, or edit the list, e.g. +ss01,-liga.

faqs.q: Can it make a static font from a variable font?
faqs.a: Yes. Pin every axis (for example wght=700 wdth=100 opsz=drop) to get a static instance, or limit an axis (wght=400:700) to keep a smaller variable font.

faqs.q: Is it legal to subset my font?
faqs.a: That depends on the font license. The tool shows the license fields and warns when the font's fsType bits forbid embedding or subsetting. Open-licensed fonts (SIL OFL, Apache) allow it.

faqs.q: Does it upload my fonts?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs locally with fontTools on 127.0.0.1; there is no network access.

tools.name: Pandoc GUI
tools.description: Convert documents between Markdown, DOCX, HTML, EPUB, LaTeX and PDF with pandoc.
tools.engine_reason: Official Pandoc binaries preserve document structure across formats; Typst creates offline PDFs without a TeX distribution.
tools.release_notes: Round-2 fixes: citations always use an explicit job-folder style (uploaded CSL or bundled Chicago author-date); document csl/citation-style/citation-abbreviations/bibliography metadata ignored; dependent CSL parents matched by id among uploaded/bundled styles only, never fetched; text writers keep RST titles/docinfo (output matches pandoc defaults); --csl repeatable.

howto: Install Pandoc GUI and run localtools-pandoc-gui to open its local page.
Paste text, or add documents with their images. A folder or ZIP preserves relative resource paths; checked documents are converted in order.
Choose an output format. Add contents, citations or a reference document when needed, then Convert and Download.
For scripts, use localtools-pandoc-gui convert input.md -o output.docx; PDFs work without a separate LaTeX install.

faqs.q: Do PDFs need a LaTeX installation?
faqs.a: No. The ZIP includes Typst 0.15.1 and its built-in fonts. Pandoc converts document structure to Typst, then Typst makes the PDF.

faqs.q: Will a DOCX or LaTeX document keep exactly the same layout?
faqs.a: Pandoc preserves structure rather than page layout. Complex tables and styling can change; PDFs use Typst layout. DOCX, ODT and PPTX outputs can take a reference document for styles.

faqs.q: Does conversion use the network?
faqs.a: No engines or fonts are fetched after install. Upload images and included files with the document. Remote images and Typst packages are unavailable; the HTML preview blocks external resources and scripts.

faqs.q: What are the web limits?
faqs.a: 256 MiB for the entire multipart request, 2,000 files, 512 MiB extracted ZIP content, 120 seconds and two simultaneous conversions. Large HTML results download normally but preview only below 20 MiB.

faqs.q: Can it read PDFs, scanned pages or legacy .doc files?
faqs.a: No. PDF is an output format; OCR and legacy binary Word input are cut. Use DOCX, ODT, HTML, EPUB, text markup, spreadsheets or presentations supported by Pandoc.

tools.name: Typst Editor
tools.description: Write Typst documents with live preview and export them to PDF, PNG or SVG.
tools.engine_reason: The official typst binary compiles in milliseconds and needs nothing else.
tools.release_notes: First release: live preview, clickable diagnostics, PDF/PDF-A/PNG/SVG export, zip projects; bundles typst 0.15.1; never downloads packages.

howto: Start it: the editor opens with an article template and its live preview.
Type: the preview recompiles 250 ms after you stop and only reloads pages that changed.
Open a folder, a zip or single files; double-click a .typ tab to make it the main file.
Click a diagnostic to jump to its file, line and column.
Export PDF (or PDF/A, PDF/UA), PNG or SVG pages, or download the whole project as a zip.

faqs.q: Does it need the internet?
faqs.a: No. The official typst 0.15.1 binary is bundled and every compile runs on your machine. The tool blocks typst package downloads.

faqs.q: Can I use @preview packages?
faqs.a: Packages already in your Typst package cache work. Others are never downloaded: copy the package files into your project and import them by path.

faqs.q: Are my files safe from the document?
faqs.a: Each compile runs in a fresh temporary folder set as the typst root, so a document cannot read files outside the project. Endless loops are killed after 60 seconds and memory is capped.

faqs.q: Is the PDF the same as running typst myself?
faqs.a: Yes. With the same flags and creation timestamp, the PDF is byte-identical to the typst CLI output (tested).

faqs.q: Can I use my own fonts?
faqs.a: Add .ttf or .otf files to the project; typst finds them. System fonts are used too unless you untick that option.
